feedback: If the quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 or 3605), check that every brought-down digit produced a quotient digit — write a 0 when 13 does not fit, and align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
If estimation stalls or uses random multipliers, jot or consult the multiples menu (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) and read off how many fit.
If the remainder fraction is inverted (13/7) or left as a bare 'r7', name it: 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more group, so the fraction is 7/13 — the remainder always goes over the divisor.

If one step is wrong from a subtraction/multiplication slip, don't restart the method: check your own quotient × 13 + remainder against 4752, compare with the estimate (between 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so between 300 and 400), then find and fix the faulty step.
activities.intendedInsight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.
learnerActions: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
activities.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)

feedback: If the chunks don't add up to the compact quotient, check the place value of each chunk (hundreds, tens, ones) and that you kept subtracting while a value of 13 or more remained.
If chunks feel random, start with the largest hundreds multiple that still fits (13×300 = 3900 ≤ 4752, but 13×400 = 5200 is too big), then the tens multiple, then ones.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact long-division digits are shorthand for subtracting bundles of the divisor (here 13×300, 13×60, 13×5, which give the hundreds, tens and ones digits of the quotient), so the algorithm is repeated subtraction organised by place value, not a magic routine.
learnerActions: Solve 4752 ÷ 13 by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of 13: subtract 13×300 = 3900 (leaving 852), then 13×60 = 780 (leaving 72), then 13×5 = 65 (leaving 7), keeping a running tally of how many 13s you have removed.
Add the chunk counts (300 + 60 + 5 = 365) to get the quotient, with 7 left over.
Line up the chunking record beside the compact long-division layout and match each compact step to a bundled chunk.
activities.title: Chunking (partial quotients) as a transparent bridge

feedback: If the rounding direction is wrong, re-read the context: 'buses needed' forces rounding up because the 7 leftover people still need a whole extra bus, whereas 'complete groups made' rounds down because the leftover 7 cannot make a full group.
If the fraction denominator is wrong, remember the remainder is written over the divisor (7/13), because 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more.
activities.intendedInsight: One division can give several correct answers; the context decides whether the leftover is a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding up or down.
learnerActions: Take the result 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 and express the remainder three ways: as the fraction 7/13, as a decimal (≈0.54, giving ≈365.54), and as a rounded whole number.

Match each interpretation to a context: e.g. sharing a divisible quantity such as 4752 g of flour equally into 13 bags (fraction/decimal), versus a context where you must round up (e.g. how many buses/containers are needed), versus one where you round down (e.g. complete full groups made).
State and justify which interpretation each context demands and why rounding up or down fits.
activities.title: Interpreting the remainder for three contexts

feedback: If the estimate and the answer differ wildly, a quotient digit or a zero place is probably misplaced — recheck alignment.
If the inverse check fails, a subtraction or multiplication slip occurred in one step; find and fix that step rather than restarting.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first catches place-value errors, and multiplying back verifies the answer; being able to say what each step does distinguishes understanding from copying a routine.
learnerActions: Estimate the quotient before dividing (e.g. 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so 4752÷13 is between 300 and 400; 4800÷13 ≈ 370 is a closer estimate, while 4800÷12 = 400 is a rougher overestimate) to anchor the leading digit.

After completing the division, voice what one specific step does — e.g. 'when I bring down the 5, what number am I now dividing by 13?' (answer: the brought-down value, here 85, since 47÷13 left 8 and the 5 comes down beside it).
Verify the full result by multiplying quotient×divisor and adding the remainder (365×13 + 7 = 4752).
activities.title: Check and explain each step
